blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 7 (Waves and Vibrations), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is a wave? Define amplitude, frequency, wavelength, period and phase of a wave, and derive the relation between the speed, frequency and wavelength of a wave. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Wave: a regular disturbance or variation that carries energy, which spreads out from the source. In a medium the particles move up and down or to and fro at their own places while the pattern spreads (e.g. ripples on a pond).

Displacement of a particle: its distance in a specified direction from its rest / equilibrium position. Plotting displacement (y-axis) against distance in the direction of energy travel (x-axis) gives the waveform (Fig. 7.2).

Parameters:
1. Amplitude (A): the maximum displacement of the wave (or particles of the medium) from its equilibrium position.
2. Frequency (f): the number of oscillations/vibrations or cycles per second.
3. Wavelength (λ): the distance between two consecutive similar points on the wave that are in phase.
4. Period (T): the time taken to complete one oscillation or cycle; T = 1/f.
5. Phase (θ): the relative position of a point on the wave at a given time.

Speed of a wave: A wave crest moves one wavelength λ in one period T, so
v = λ/T
As 1/T = f,
v = fλ ... (7.1)

book_ref.quote: The waves can be described by the following parameters:

blocks.prompt: 2 A radio transmitter operating at 1.2 MHz sends waves of wavelength 250 m. Find (i) the speed of the radio waves (ii) the wavelength of a second transmitter operating at 600 kHz (iii) the period of the first wave. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both signals travel at the same speed; use v = fλ, then λ = v/f and T = 1/f.

book_ref.quote: What is the wavelength for a transmitter operating at 1000 kHz

steps: f₁ = 1.2 MHz = 1.2 × 10⁶ Hz, λ₁ = 250 m, f₂ = 600 kHz = 6.0 × 10⁵ Hz

blocks.prompt: 3 State the principle of superposition of waves. Explain the resultant displacement when two overlapping waves are (i) in the same phase (ii) in opposite phase, and extend the principle to n waves. Which phenomena does it lead to? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Principle: If a particle of the medium is simultaneously acted upon by two waves, the resultant displacement of the particle is the algebraic sum of their individual displacements. The displacements are added to form a new wave pattern (Fig. 7.4).

(i) Same phase (Fig. 7.4 a):
y = y₁ + y₂
If y₁ = y₂, then y = 2y₁ (or 2y₂): a larger resultant.

(ii) Opposite phase (Fig. 7.4 b):
y = y₁ + (−y₂) = y₁ − y₂
If y₁ = y₂, then y = 0: the waves cancel.

n waves: if the displacements due to n waves are y₁, y₂, …, yₙ, the resultant displacement is
y = y₁ + y₂ + … + yₙ
or, as wave functions, y(x,t) = y₁(x,t) + y₂(x,t) + … + yₙ(x,t), where y(x,t) is the resultant displacement at point x and time t.
The principle applies to linear waves, that is, waves of small amplitude.

Phenomena:
1. Same frequency, same direction: interference.
2. Slightly different frequencies, same direction: beats.
3. Equal frequency, opposite directions: stationary waves.

book_ref.quote: In other words, the displacements of the individual waves are added together to form a new wave pattern

blocks.prompt: 4 Find the resultant displacement of a particle when (i) two waves of displacement 4 mm each meet in the same phase (ii) the same two waves meet in opposite phase (iii) three waves give displacements of +6 mm, −2 mm and +3 mm at the same instant. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Add the displacements algebraically: same phase adds, opposite phase subtracts.

book_ref.quote: where y₁ = amplitude of wave 1, y₂ = amplitude of wave 2 and y = resultant amplitude.

steps: (i) Same phase, y₁ = y₂: y = 2y₁ = 2 × 4 = 8 mm
(ii) Opposite phase, y₁ = y₂: y = y₁ − y₂ = 4 − 4 = 0

blocks.prompt: 5 Define interference. Describe an experiment with two loudspeakers and a CRO to observe interference of sound waves, and obtain the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of path difference. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Interference: superposition of two waves having the same frequency and travelling in the same direction.

Apparatus (Fig. 7.5 a): Two loudspeakers S₁ and S₂ are driven by the same Audio Generator (AG), so they emit harmonic sound waves of a fixed frequency and vibrate in phase (coherent sources). A microphone connected to a sensitive Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO) detects the sound; the CRO displays the signal as a waveform. The microphone is placed at various points in front of the speakers (Fig. 7.5 b).

Constructive interference: At P₁, P₃ and P₅ a compression meets a compression and a rarefaction meets a rarefaction. The displacements add and a large displacement is seen on the CRO (Fig. 7.5 c). At P₁:
ΔS = S₂P₁ − S₁P₁ = 4½λ − 3½λ = λ
At P₃ and P₅, ΔS = 0 and −λ. So whenever the path difference is an integral multiple of wavelength:
ΔS = nλ, where n = 0, ±1, ±2, ±3, …

Destructive interference: At P₂ and P₄ a compression meets a rarefaction; they cancel and the CRO shows zero displacement (Fig. 7.5 d). At P₂:
ΔS = S₂P₂ − S₁P₂ = 4λ − 3½λ = ½λ
So the path difference is an odd integral multiple of half the wavelength:
ΔS = (2n + 1)λ/2, where n = 0, ±1, ±2, ±3, …

book_ref.quote: An experimental set up to observe interference effect of sound waves is shown in Fig. 7.5(a).

blocks.prompt: 6 Two loudspeakers 1.2 m apart are driven by the same generator at 850 Hz. A microphone moved along a line parallel to and 1.6 m from the line joining the speakers gives maximum loudness at the centre and again when it is directly opposite one speaker. Find the wavelength and the speed of sound. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Directly opposite S₁ is the next loud point after the centre, so the path difference there is λ; find S₂P by Pythagoras.

book_ref.quote: Now, we calculate values of S₂P₁ from right angle triangle S₁S₂P₁

steps: S₁S₂ = 1.2 m, S₁P = 1.6 m, f = 850 Hz

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain how stationary waves are formed by two waves moving along a string in opposite directions. Show that nodes are λ/2 apart and that a node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart. How is energy held in a stationary wave? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Stationary (standing) waves oscillate in a fixed position without propagating. They are formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions; nodes and antinodes stay at fixed positions.

Formation (Fig. 7.6): Figures 7.6 (a) and (b) show two such waves on a string at t = 0, T/4, T/2, 3T/4 and T. Points 1, 2, …, 7 are λ/4 apart. Their resultant displacements are found by the principle of superposition.

Nodes: Fig. 7.6 (c) shows that the resultant displacement of points 1, 3, 5 and 7 is always zero at all these instants. These points are nodes. Points 1 and 3 are two steps of λ/4 apart, so the distance between consecutive nodes is λ/2.

Antinodes: Fig. 7.6 (d) shows that points 2, 4 and 6 move with an amplitude equal to the sum of the amplitudes of the component waves. These are antinodes, midway between the nodes and λ/2 apart. The distance between a node and the next antinode is λ/4.

Energy: Energy in a wave transfers because of the motion of the particles. The nodes always remain at rest, so energy cannot flow past them; it remains 'standing' between nodes. At the antinodes it alternates: wholly potential when the antinodes are at their extreme displacements, wholly kinetic when they pass through their equilibrium positions together.

book_ref.quote: Let us consider the superposition of two waves moving along a string in opposite directions.

blocks.prompt: 8 Two waves, each of amplitude 3 mm, frequency 80 Hz and speed 48 m s⁻¹, travel along a string in opposite directions and form a stationary wave. Find (i) the wavelength (ii) the distance between consecutive nodes (iii) the distance between a node and the next antinode (iv) the amplitude at an antinode. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find λ from v = fλ, then use λ/2 and λ/4; the antinode amplitude is the sum of the two amplitudes.

book_ref.quote: They are situated midway between the nodes and are λ/2 apart.

steps: Node to next antinode = λ/4 = 0.60/4 = 0.15 m

blocks.prompt: 9 A string of length l is stretched by clamping its ends with tension F. Explain the stationary waves set up when it is plucked (i) at its middle point (ii) at one quarter of its length, and derive the frequency in each case. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Consider a string of length l kept stretched by clamping its ends so that its tension is F.

(i) Plucked at the middle point (Fig. 7.7 a): Two transverse waves start from the middle, one towards each end. At the clamped ends they reflect back, giving stationary waves. No motion takes place at the clamped ends, so nodes form there with one antinode in between: the string vibrates in one loop. The distance between two consecutive nodes is λ/2, so
l = λ₁/2
λ₁ = 2l ... (7.2)
The speed of waves on the string depends on the tension F and mass per unit length m (not on the point of plucking):
v = √(F/m) ... (7.3)
f₁ = v/λ₁ = v/2l
f₁ = (1/2l)√(F/m) ... (7.4)

(ii) Plucked at one quarter of its length (Fig. 7.7 b): The string is plucked at the position of an antinode, so it vibrates in two loops. Each loop is λ₂/2 long:
l = λ₂/2 + λ₂/2 = 2(λ₂/2)
λ₂ = l
The wavelength is half of that in the first case. The speed v is the same (it depends only on F and m), so
f₂ = v/λ₂ = v/l
Multiplying and dividing by 2: f₂ = 2v/2l
Since f₁ = v/2l, f₂ = 2f₁
Thus in two loops the frequency is double that in one loop.

book_ref.quote: If the string is plucked at its middle point, two transverse waves will originate from this point.

blocks.prompt: 10 A string 0.80 m long has a mass per unit length of 0.010 kg m⁻¹ and is stretched with a tension of 64 N. Find (i) the speed of transverse waves on it (ii) its fundamental frequency (iii) its frequency when plucked at one quarter of its length. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Get v from √(F/m), then f₁ = v/2l; quarter-length plucking gives two loops, f₂ = 2f₁.

book_ref.quote: Knowing the speed v and wavelength λ₁, the frequency f₁ of the waves is

steps: Plucked at quarter length: two loops, f₂ = 2f₁ = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz
blocks.final_answer: v = 80 m s⁻¹; f₁ = 50 Hz; f₂ = 100 Hz

blocks.prompt: 11 Show that a stretched string vibrating in n loops has frequency fₙ = nf₁ and wavelength λₙ = 2l/n. Explain the harmonic series, quantization of frequencies, and how the frequency of a string on a musical instrument is changed. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Let the string resonate in n loops, with (n + 1) nodes and n antinodes. Each loop is the distance between two consecutive nodes, λₙ/2, so
l = n(λₙ/2)
λₙ = 2l/n ... (7.6)
The speed v = √(F/m) is the same for every mode, so
fₙ = v/λₙ = n(v/2l)
fₙ = nf₁ ... (7.5), or fₙ ∝ n, where n = 1, 2, 3, …
As the string vibrates in more loops, f increases and λ gets shorter, but the product fλ always equals v.

Harmonic series: The stationary waves have a discrete set of frequencies f₁, 2f₁, 3f₁, …, nf₁. The lowest, f₁, is the fundamental frequency (first harmonic); f₂ = 2f₁ is the second harmonic, and so on.

Quantization of frequencies: Quantum jumps in frequency exist between the resonance frequencies; fₙ = nf₁ with n an integer. Stationary waves can be set up only with these frequencies, determined by the tension, length and mass per unit length; waves not in the harmonic series are quickly damped out.

Musical instruments: The frequency is changed by varying the tension (tightening the pegs of a guitar or violin) or by changing the length (moving the fingers along the neck to change the length of the vibrating portion).

book_ref.quote: Thus, we can say that if the string is made to vibrate in n loops

blocks.prompt: 12 A string 1.5 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in three segments at a frequency of 150 Hz. Find (i) the wavelength (ii) the fundamental frequency (iii) the speed of the waves (iv) the number of nodes and antinodes. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Three segments means n = 3: use λₙ = 2l/n, fₙ = nf₁ and v = fλ; n loops have (n + 1) nodes and n antinodes.

book_ref.quote: (ii) If string vibrates in n loops, then frequency of stationary waves will be:

blocks.final_answer: λ = 1.0 m; f₁ = 50 Hz; v = 150 m s⁻¹; 4 nodes, 3 antinodes

blocks.prompt: 13 What is an organ pipe? For an organ pipe of length l open at both ends, derive the frequencies of the fundamental mode, the second mode and the nth mode of vibration. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Organ pipe: a wind instrument in which sound is produced by stationary waves set up in the air column of a hollow long tube (both ends open, or one end open and the other closed). An open reflecting end is an antinode (air molecules are free to move); a closed end is a node (their movement is restricted).

Pipe open at both ends (Fig. 7.8): Both ends are antinodes. The longitudinal waves in the pipe are drawn as transverse curves showing displacement and amplitude of the air particles.

(a) Fundamental mode: one node N at the middle, antinodes at both ends:
l = λ₁/4 + λ₁/4 = λ₁/2
λ₁ = 2l ... (7.7)
v = f₁λ₁ → f₁ = v/λ₁
f₁ = v/2l ... (7.8)
This is the fundamental frequency or first harmonic.

(b) Second mode: three antinodes and two nodes (Fig. 7.8 b):
l = λ₂/4 + λ₂/2 + λ₂/4 = (1 + 2 + 1)λ₂/4
λ₂ = l
f₂ = v/λ₂ = v/l = 2f₁ (since v/2l = f₁)

(c) nth mode:
fₙ = n(v/2l) = nf₁
λₙ = 2l/n ... (7.9), where n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …
So an open pipe gives the harmonic series f₁, 2f₁, 3f₁, …, nf₁ (all harmonics).

book_ref.quote: As at the open end, an air molecule has complete freedom of motion so it acts as antinode

blocks.prompt: 14 An organ pipe 0.85 m long is open at both ends. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹, find the wavelength and frequency of the fundamental, and the frequencies of the second and third harmonics. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: For an open pipe λ₁ = 2l, f₁ = v/2l and fₙ = nf₁ with n = 1, 2, 3, …

book_ref.quote: Similarly, frequency for air column vibrating in n loops is:

blocks.final_answer: λ₁ = 1.7 m; f₁ = 200 Hz; f₂ = 400 Hz; f₃ = 600 Hz

blocks.prompt: 15 For an organ pipe of length l closed at one end, derive the frequencies of the fundamental mode, the second mode and the nth mode of vibration. Why is a pipe open at both ends richer in harmonics? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
In a pipe closed at one end (Fig. 7.9) the closed end is a node (movement of air molecules restricted) and the open end is an antinode.

(a) Fundamental mode: one node and one antinode (Fig. 7.9 a):
l = λ₁/4
λ₁ = 4l ... (7.10)
v = f₁λ₁ → f₁ = v/λ₁ = v/4l
f₁ is the fundamental frequency.

(b) Second mode: two nodes and two antinodes (Fig. 7.9 b):
l = λ₃/4 + λ₃/2 = (3/4)λ₃
λ₃ = 4l/3 ... (7.11)
f₃ = v/λ₃ = v/(4l/3) = 3v/4l
f₃ = 3f₁ (since v/4l = f₁)
Its harmonic number is f/f₁ = 3, so the second mode gives the third harmonic.

(c) nth mode:
fₙ = n(v/4l) = nf₁
λₙ = 4l/n ... (7.12), where n = 1, 3, 5, …
Only odd harmonics are present.

Comparison: An open pipe gives fₙ = nf₁ with n = 1, 2, 3, … (all harmonics), but a closed pipe gives only n = 1, 3, 5, … So the pipe open at both ends is richer in harmonics.

book_ref.quote: Then at the closed end, we get a node while at the open end, we get an antinode

blocks.prompt: 16 An organ pipe 0.17 m long is closed at one end. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹, find the wavelength of its fundamental mode and the frequencies of its first three modes of vibration. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: For a closed pipe λ₁ = 4l and fₙ = nf₁ with only odd n = 1, 3, 5, …

book_ref.quote: When the pipe is closed at one end then frequency for nth harmonic is:

blocks.prompt: 17 What are microwaves? Describe an experiment to demonstrate stationary waves using microwaves, and explain how the wavelength is found from it. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Microwaves: a form of electromagnetic radiation. They are called 'micro' waves because their wavelengths are typically of the order of millimetres or centimetres, much shorter than radiowaves.

Stationary microwaves: When microwaves are confined to a region or cavity (wave guides, resonant chambers), they bounce back and forth and create a standing wave with nodes and antinodes. This happens when the microwave frequency matches the resonant frequency of the cavity.

Experiment (Fig. 7.10):
Apparatus: a microwave source (transmitter), a probe detector and a metal reflector (metallic plate), placed in line.
1. Waves from the source travel to the metal plate and are reflected back.
2. The reflected wave and the incident wave superpose and create a stationary wave pattern.
3. The probe detector, placed between the transmitter and the plate, detects it; the intensity of the signal is observed by the detector.
4. Moving the plate or the detector, positions of maximum signal (antinodes) and minimum signal (nodes) are found.

Wavelength: The distance from one antinode to the next antinode is measured. Since antinodes are λ/2 apart (7.4), λ = 2 × (antinode-to-antinode distance).

book_ref.quote: The waves coming out of microwave source are moving towards the metal plate and then reflected back.

blocks.prompt: 18 In a microwave stationary wave experiment, the probe detector is moved from one antinode past four further antinodes, a total distance of 6.0 cm. Find the wavelength and frequency of the microwaves (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Moving past four further antinodes covers four antinode-to-antinode gaps of λ/2 each.

book_ref.quote: By finding the distance from one antinode to the next antinode

blocks.prompt: 19 How does the size of an opening compared with the wavelength affect the diffraction of waves? Explain with the observations in a ripple tank and give two examples of diffraction from everyday life and science. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Diffraction: the bending of waves around the sharp edges or corners of obstacles, or the spreading of waves beyond a barrier. It occurs when a wave meets a barrier or an opening (slit) comparable in size to its wavelength. The longer the wavelength, the greater the spreading, and vice versa. It is seen in water, sound, light and other electromagnetic waves.

Ripple tank (Fig. 7.11): It contains water, a vibrator (e.g. a motorized oscillating needle), obstacles (a small rectangular block or semicircular barrier) and gaps of different widths. The vibrator makes concentric circular or parallel waves; an obstacle is placed to make a gap of a chosen width and the experiment is repeated with different gap widths.

Observations:
1. Gap width small compared to the wavelength: diffraction is significant; the waves bend around and form a semicircular pattern.
2. Gap width increased relative to wavelength: diffraction decreases; the waves pass through with less bending.
So the relationship between gap width and wavelength controls wave behaviour.

Examples:
(i) Sound is heard around corners or through a door way because sound waves bend around corners.
(ii) X-rays are diffracted by crystals because the spacing between the regular arrays of atoms is of the order of the X-ray wavelength.

book_ref.quote: It occurs when a wave encounters a physical barrier or an opening (a slit)

blocks.prompt: 20 The vibrator of a ripple tank produces 360 pulses in 12 s, and the distance between successive crests is 2.0 cm. Find (i) the period (ii) the frequency (iii) the speed of the water waves. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Period is time per pulse; frequency is its reciprocal; the crest spacing is the wavelength, so v = fλ.

book_ref.quote: n = 500 pulses t = 10 s f = ?

blocks.prompt: 21 Explain, with the example of two tuning forks of 32 Hz and 28 Hz, how beats are produced and why the number of beats per second equals the frequency difference. How are beats used to find an unknown frequency or to tune an instrument? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Beats: when two waves of slightly different frequencies travelling in the same direction overlap, there is a periodic variation of sound between maximum and minimum loudness, called beats.

Production: Tuning forks give pure notes. Two forks A and B of the same frequency (32 Hz) sounded together are heard as a single pure note. If B is loaded with wax or plasticene its frequency is lowered, say to 28 Hz. Sounded together, they give a note of alternately increasing and decreasing intensity, the beat note, due to interference of their sound waves.

Waveforms (Fig. 7.12): (a) shows the wave of A, (b) the wave of B and (c) their resultant.
• At instant X the displacements of the two waves are in the same direction: large resultant, loud sound.
• 1/8 s later, at Y, the displacements are opposite: minimum resultant, faint or no sound.
• Another 1/8 s later, at Z, they are again in the same direction: loud sound again.
So one loud sound to the next takes 1/4 s, i.e. 4 beats per second.

Beats per second: The difference of frequencies is fA − fB = 32 Hz − 28 Hz = 4 Hz, the same as the number of beats per second. Hence
number of beats per second = fA − fB, and f_beat = 1/T, where T = t₂ − t₁ is the time between two successive loud sounds.
When the frequency difference is more than 10 Hz, beats are difficult to recognize.

Uses:
(i) Unknown frequency: sound the unknown fork with a known one; f₂ = f₁ ± (beats per second). Loading one fork with wax lowers its frequency; whether the beats then increase or decrease shows which value is correct.
(ii) Tuning: a piano or violin string is sounded against a note of known frequency and tightened or loosened until no beats are heard.

book_ref.quote: This note is called beat note or a beat which is due to interference between the sound waves

blocks.prompt: 22 A tuning fork A of frequency 384 Hz produces 5 beats per second with another fork B. When B is loaded with a little wax, the beat frequency falls to 3 beats per second. Find (i) the frequency of B before loading (ii) the time between two successive loud sounds before loading. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: B has two possible values, fA ± 5; wax lowers B, so keep the value for which lowering B brings it closer to 384 Hz.

book_ref.quote: When first fork is loaded with wax, the frequency of first fork must fall below 256 Hz

steps: Wax lowers fB. If fB = 379 Hz it moves further from 384 Hz and beats would increase above 5.
If fB = 389 Hz it moves towards 384 Hz and beats decrease (to 3), as observed; so fB = 389 Hz

blocks.prompt: 23 Define intensity of a wave and state its unit. Show that I = P/A, and explain why the intensity of a mechanical wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude. What is a progressive wave? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Progressive wave: a wave that travels through a medium in a consistent direction, transferring energy from one point to another, as opposed to a stationary wave. Examples: water waves, sound waves, light waves.

Intensity: the amount of energy transmitted per unit area per unit time in the direction of propagation of a progressive wave. It is a measure of the power of a wave, denoted by I, and measured in watts per square meter (W m⁻²).

Expression: By definition,
I = E/(A × t)
I = (E/t)/A
I = P/A (since E/t = P)
where E = energy (J), t = time (s), P = power (W), A = area (m²). For waves spreading evenly in all directions from a source, A is the surface area of a sphere, 4πr², so I = P/(4πr²).

Intensity and amplitude: In mechanical waves (sound waves, water waves, waves on a string), energy is stored as kinetic energy and potential energy of the medium's particles. How much energy is stored depends upon the displacement (amplitude) of the particles from the mean position. Therefore
I ∝ A²
I = kA² ... (7.13)
where k is a constant that depends upon the physical properties of the wave and the medium.

Note: frequency and amplitude of a travelling wave are independent, so loudness can rise (amplitude) without changing pitch (frequency).

book_ref.quote: Intensity is defined as the amount of energy transmitted per unit area per unit time

blocks.prompt: 24 A small source emits 80 W of sound evenly in all directions. Find (i) the area of the sphere at 4.0 m (ii) the intensity at 4.0 m (iii) the intensity at that point if the amplitude of the waves there were doubled. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Spread the power over 4πr², then use I ∝ A² for the change in amplitude.
steps: I = kA²: doubling the amplitude makes I four times: I′ = 4 × 0.398 = 1.6 W m⁻²

blocks.prompt: 25 What is the Doppler effect? Derive an expression for the apparent frequency heard by a stationary observer when a source of sound moves towards the observer, and show that the pitch rises. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Doppler effect: the apparent change in the frequency (or pitch) of waves due to the relative motion between the source and the observer (listener). Example: the whistle of an engine coming towards a platform sounds higher; going away it sounds lower.

Source at rest: A source S at rest emits waves of wavelength λ with speed v. The number of waves received by a stationary observer per second is
f = v/λ

Source moving towards stationary observer C with velocity uₛ (Fig. 7.12): The waves are compressed because the same number of waves are contained in a shorter space. The decrease in wavelength in one second (Doppler shift) is
Δλ = uₛ/f
Wavelength observed by C:
λ_C = λ − Δλ
λ_C = v/f − uₛ/f
λ_C = (v − uₛ)/f
Apparent frequency (number of waves received by C per second):
f_C = v/λ_C
f_C = v/[(v − uₛ)/f]
f_C = [v/(v − uₛ)] f

As v/(v − uₛ) > 1, f_C > f. The apparent frequency heard by the observer increases, so the pitch of the sound increases.

book_ref.quote: The compression of the waves is due to the fact that same number of waves are contained in a shorter space

blocks.prompt: 26 A motorcycle horn of frequency 620 Hz approaches a stationary listener at 30 m s⁻¹ (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). Find (i) the Doppler shift Δλ (ii) the wavelength reaching the listener (iii) the frequency heard. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use Δλ = uₛ/f, then λ_C = (v − uₛ)/f and f_C = v/λ_C.

book_ref.quote: Putting the value of λ_C, we have

blocks.prompt: 27 Derive an expression for the apparent frequency heard by a stationary observer when a source of sound moves away from the observer, and show that the pitch falls. Compare the result with the case of an approaching source. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Let a source emit waves of frequency f and wavelength λ = v/f, where v is the speed of sound.

Source moving away from stationary observer D with velocity uₛ (Fig. 7.12): The waves are expanded, because the same number of waves are now contained in a larger distance. The increase in wavelength in one second (Doppler shift) is
Δλ = uₛ/f
Wavelength observed by D:
λ_D = λ + Δλ
λ_D = v/f + uₛ/f = (v + uₛ)/f
Apparent frequency (number of waves received by D per second):
f_D = v/λ_D
f_D = v/[(v + uₛ)/f]
f_D = [v/(v + uₛ)] f

As v/(v + uₛ) < 1, f_D < f. The apparent frequency heard decreases, so the pitch of the sound decreases.

Comparison: for an approaching source, λ_C = (v − uₛ)/f and f_C = [v/(v − uₛ)] f > f (pitch rises); for a receding source, λ_D = (v + uₛ)/f and f_D = [v/(v + uₛ)] f < f (pitch falls).

book_ref.quote: where Δλ is the increase in wavelength in one second and is called Doppler shift.

blocks.prompt: 29 Describe the applications of the Doppler effect in (i) RADAR (ii) SONAR (iii) astronomy (red shift and blue shift) (iv) the radar speed trap. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The Doppler effect applies to electromagnetic waves as well as sound.

(i) RADAR (RAdio Detection And Ranging): a device that transmits and receives radio waves to determine the elevation and speed of an aeroplane. If the aeroplane approaches the radar, the reflected wavelength is shorter; if it moves away, longer (Fig. 7.13). The speed of satellites around the Earth is found by the same principle.

(ii) SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging): sonic or ultrasonic underwater echo-ranging; it detects objects under water by acoustical echo. Doppler detection uses the relative speed of target and detector to indicate the target's speed. Military uses: detecting and locating submarines, controlling antisubmarine weapons, mine hunting; also depth measurement of the sea.

(iii) Astronomy: the line spectrum of a star is compared with a laboratory source to measure the Doppler shift, and from it the star's speed.
• Stars moving away show a red shift: longer wavelength, spectrum shifted to the red end. All distant galaxies show red shifts, so they are moving away from us.
• Stars moving towards the Earth show a blue shift: shorter wavelength, spectrum shifted to the blue end (Fig. 7.14).

(iv) Radar speed trap: microwaves are emitted in short bursts and reflected by a car in their path. Reflections from a moving car are Doppler shifted; by measuring the shift, a computer programme calculates the car's speed.

Other uses: satellite navigation and communication, Doppler radar for wind and precipitation, Doppler ultrasound and echocardiography for blood flow.

book_ref.quote: Doppler effect is also applicable to electromagnetic waves.
